title: Intel raises $20 billion in first common-stock offering since 1971 to fund AI-driven capex
subtitle: The chipmaker announced a $15B underwritten offering on August 10 and upsized to $20B at $95 a share the next morning, banking on AI demand to justify triple-digit share prices and heavy foundry spend.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Intel announced a $15 billion underwritten public offering of common stock on August 10 and, early on August 11, priced and upsized the deal to $20 billion at $95 per share. It is the company's first common-share sale since its 1971 IPO. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and Citigroup are joint book-runners. The stock had nearly tripled in 2026 before the offering, and Intel said proceeds go to general corporate purposes including capex — foundry buildout, advanced packaging, physical-AI silicon and external wafer capacity.

The size of the raise matters. Intel has spent the last three years pouring cash into fabs while its data-center CPU business shrank against AMD and Nvidia. Equity, not debt, is the tell: the company is choosing to dilute existing shareholders rather than add more interest expense to already stretched cash flow, and it can do so at $95 because investors have decided the foundry story is finally credible. Winning even a handful of external AI-accelerator customers on 18A or 14A would validate the thesis; missing on execution would leave Intel with more capacity than customers.

This is the second time in three weeks that AI capital demand has visibly bent public markets — after last month's SK Hynix Nasdaq debut and the September 2025 SpaceXAI IPO plans, the pattern is clear: chip and infrastructure companies are raising unprecedented amounts of equity to keep pace with hyperscaler and frontier-lab orders. Intel's raise also gives it flexibility on the Anthropic-Google-Broadcom style deals its rivals have been signing — deals where the customer effectively pre-funds capacity. With $20B fresh on the balance sheet, Intel can negotiate from a stronger position.

For learners: when you read that a public company is issuing equity into a hot market, ask who is really paying. Existing shareholders pay via dilution; new shareholders pay a premium bet that management will deploy the cash productively. In AI infrastructure, the specific bet is that the customer (a hyperscaler, a frontier lab, a sovereign) will actually take delivery at the promised volumes. Following that chain — who's committing capital, to whom, on what terms — is more predictive of the AI cycle than any benchmark.
